content: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) is a condition characterized by inflammation affecting various parts of the body, including the heart, blood vessels, kidneys, digestive system, brain, skin, or eyes. Evidence suggests that children with MIS-C have antibodies against COVID-19, indicating a prior infection with the virus. This syndrome shares clinical similarities with Kawasaki disease and is sometimes referred to as a Kawasaki-like disease. It also overlaps with features of staphylococcal and streptococcal toxic shock syndromes, bacterial sepsis, and macrophage activation syndromes. Classification of Disease Severity in MIS-C: 1. Mild Disease: Children require minimal to no respiratory support. There is minimal to no organ injury, and they remain normotensive. These patients do not meet criteria for ICU admission. 2. Severe Disease: Children have significant oxygen requirements, such as high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC), BiPAP, or mechanical ventilation. They may exhibit mild to severe organ injury, including ventricular dysfunction. Vasoactive support is often required. These patients meet criteria for ICU admission. Pathophysiology: The exact mechanism underlying MIS-C remains unclear. However, the delayed onset of MIS-C following COVID-19 infection suggests a role for antibody-dependent enhancement. Another hypothesis involves the suppression of type I and type III interferons by the coronavirus, leading to a delayed cytokine response. This delay may result in a cytokine storm in children with high viral loads or an inadequate immune response, causing multisystem inflammation. Additionally, the predominant gastrointestinal symptoms in MIS-C suggest viral replication in the gastrointestinal tract. Differential Diagnosis: MIS-C must be differentiated from other conditions, including: Bacterial sepsis Staphylococcal and streptococcal toxic shock syndromes Kawasaki disease Epidemiology and Demographics: A study of 186 children with MIS-C revealed hospitalization rates of 12% between March 16 and April 15, and 88% between April 16 and May 20. 80% of these children required ICU admission, 20% required mechanical ventilation, and 4% required extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). The mortality rate was 2%. Age Distribution: <1 year: 7% 1–4 years: 28% 5–9 years: 25% 10–14 years: 24% 15–20 years: 16% Comorbidities: Clinically diagnosed obesity: 8% BMI-based obesity: 29% Cardiovascular disease: 3% Respiratory disease: 18% Autoimmune or immunocompromising conditions: 5% Organ System Involvement: 71% of children had involvement of at least four organ systems. Most commonly affected systems: Gastrointestinal (92%) Cardiovascular (80%) Hematologic (76%) Mucocutaneous (74%) Pulmonary (70%) Complications and Prognosis: Severe complications include: Myocardial infarction Cardiac failure or arrest Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) Hypervolemia Acute kidney injury Peritonitis Thrombotic complications Diagnosis: Diagnostic criteria for MIS-C include: Age 0–19 years with fever lasting >3 days AND: Two or more of the following: Rash or bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis or mucocutaneous inflammation (oral, hands, or feet) Hypotension or shock Myocardial dysfunction, pericarditis, valvulitis, or coronary abnormalities (e.g., echocardiographic findings or elevated troponin/NT-proBNP) Evidence of coagulopathy (elevated PT, PTT, or D-dimers) Acute gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain) Elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., ESR, CRP, or procalcitonin) No other obvious microbial cause of inflammation (e.g., bacterial sepsis, staphylococcal or streptococcal shock syndromes) Evidence of COVID-19 infection (positive RT-PCR, antigen test, or serology) or recent exposure to a confirmed COVID-19 case within 4 weeks of symptom onset. Signs and Symptoms: Fever lasting ≥24 hours Vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain Skin rash, conjunctivitis High ESR, redness/swelling of lips and tongue Lethargy, redness/swelling of hands or feet Confusion, headache, sore throat, syncope Lymphadenopathy Emergency Warning Signs: Difficulty breathing Chest pain New-onset confusion Lethargy Cyanosis Severe abdominal pain Physical Examination and Laboratory Findings: Blood investigations often reveal lymphopenia, neutrophilia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Abnormal fibrinogen, hypoalbuminemia, elevated creatine kinase (CK), LDH, and triglycerides are common. Inflammatory biomarkers such as ESR, CRP, procalcitonin, IL-6, IL-10, D-dimer, serum ferritin, and prolonged prothrombin time are elevated. Cardiac biomarkers, including cardiac troponins (cTnI, cTnT) and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), are elevated. Radiological Findings: Radiological studies often exclude other potential causative organisms. SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgM levels are typically detected. Treatment: 1. Medical Therapy: All children with MIS-C are treated as suspected COVID-19 cases. Mild to moderate cases are managed supportively. Supplemental oxygen is provided for low oxygen saturation. Fluid resuscitation is performed in 10 mL/kg aliquots with careful re-evaluation to maintain euvolemia and avoid hypervolemia. Anti-inflammatory treatments, such as intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) with or without corticosteroids, have shown good response rates. Aspirin is recommended for its antiplatelet effects in all MIS-C patients. Anakinra or tocilizumab may be considered if fever persists >24 hours post-steroids/IVIG or in moderate to severe cases. Empiric antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, ceftriaxone, clindamycin) are administered for community-acquired shock presentations until cultures are negative for 48 hours. Prevention: MIS-C can be prevented by minimizing children’s exposure to COVID-19 infection.
